title: Acute angle-closure crisis (acute angle-closure glaucoma)
subject: ophthalmology-ent
summary: A painful red eye with blurred vision, haloes, a mid-dilated pupil and a stony-hard eye is acute angle closure until proven otherwise. Lower IOP immediately with acetazolamide 500 mg (IV if vomiting), topical aqueous suppressants and steroid, pilocarpine once IOP starts to fall, mannitol if needed, and arrange laser iridotomy in both eyes.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Symptoms: sudden eye pain, frontal headache, blurred vision, haloes around lights, nausea and vomiting (may mimic migraine, gastroenteritis or stroke).
Signs: red eye with ciliary injection, hazy oedematous cornea, shallow anterior chamber, fixed or sluggish mid-dilated pupil, eye rock-hard on palpation; IOP often 50 to 70 mmHg.
Risk factors: hypermetropia, older age, female sex, Asian (including Indian) ancestry, and a narrow angle in the fellow eye.
Precipitants: dim light, dilating drops, anticholinergics and sympathomimetics (nebulised ipratropium and salbutamol), antihistamines, tricyclic and some other antidepressants.
Topiramate or sulfonamides cause bilateral angle closure by ciliochoroidal effusion: stop the drug and use cycloplegia; pilocarpine and iridotomy do not help.

sections.title: Immediate IOP lowering
items: Refer immediately to ophthalmology (same-day emergency). Give analgesia and an antiemetic.
Acetazolamide 500 mg IV if IOP is 40 mmHg or more or the patient is vomiting (EGS: 10 mg/kg IV), otherwise 500 mg orally. Avoid in sulfonamide allergy, severe renal impairment and hypokalaemia.
Topical aqueous suppressants, one drop each a few minutes apart: timolol 0.5% (avoid in asthma, COPD, bradycardia or heart block) and apraclonidine 1% or brimonidine 0.2%.
Topical steroid: prednisolone acetate 1% (intensive, for example 6 times a day) to reduce inflammation.

Pilocarpine 1 to 2% one drop once IOP begins to fall (it is ineffective while the iris is ischaemic at IOP of 40 mmHg or more). Avoid intensive dosing, and do not use it in lens-induced or retro-lenticular angle closure.

If IOP remains high after about an hour: mannitol 20% 1 to 2 g/kg IV over 30 to 60 minutes (lower end in the elderly and in cardiac or renal disease), after checking for heart failure and renal impairment; or oral glycerol 1 g/kg of a 50% solution (avoid in diabetes).

sections.title: Definitive treatment
items: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) as soon as it is safely feasible, once the cornea is clear enough; topical glycerin can clear an oedematous cornea for the procedure.
Prophylactic LPI in the fellow eye promptly, ideally before discharge: about half of fellow eyes have an attack within 5 years, and pilocarpine is not a substitute.
If LPI is not possible or the attack cannot be broken medically: laser peripheral iridoplasty, anterior chamber paracentesis or surgical iridectomy.
Early lens extraction (phacoemulsification) after the attack is broken may give better long-term IOP control than LPI alone, especially with cataract.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Recheck IOP, pain and corneal clarity within an hour of starting treatment and regularly until the attack breaks.
Check electrolytes and renal function with acetazolamide or mannitol (hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis, fluid overload).
After the attack: gonioscopy of both eyes, optic disc and visual field assessment for glaucomatous damage, and long-term IOP follow-up.

sections.title: Indian context and special groups
items: Primary angle-closure disease is common in India and often presents late; check the angle before dilating older hypermetropic patients.
If IV acetazolamide is unavailable, give 500 mg orally (two 250 mg tablets) and add mannitol early if IOP stays high.
Elderly, cardiac or renal patients: mannitol can cause pulmonary oedema, heart failure and electrolyte disturbance; do not repeat it without senior advice.
Warn patients with narrow angles about drugs that dilate the pupil and to seek help for eye pain with haloes.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Missing the diagnosis in a vomiting patient with headache treated as migraine, gastroenteritis or a neurological event.
Relying on pilocarpine alone, or using it in lens-induced or drug-induced (topiramate) angle closure.
Forgetting the fellow eye.
Giving timolol to an asthmatic, acetazolamide in sulfonamide allergy, or mannitol in heart failure.

drugs.name: Acetazolamide
drugs.dose: 500 mg IV (EGS 10 mg/kg IV) or 500 mg orally stat; then 250 mg orally every 6 hours as directed by ophthalmology
drugs.notes: Avoid in sulfonamide allergy and severe renal disease; monitor potassium.

drugs.name: Timolol 0.5% eye drops
drugs.dose: 1 drop to the affected eye stat, then twice daily
drugs.notes: Avoid in asthma, COPD, bradycardia, heart block.

drugs.name: Apraclonidine 1% or brimonidine 0.2% eye drops
drugs.dose: 1 drop to the affected eye stat; further doses as directed by ophthalmology

drugs.name: Pilocarpine 1% or 2% eye drops
drugs.dose: 1 drop once IOP begins to fall; avoid intensive dosing
drugs.notes: Not for lens-induced or retro-lenticular angle closure.

drugs.name: Prednisolone acetate 1% eye drops
drugs.dose: 1 drop up to 6 times a day
drugs.notes: Reduces inflammation; taper after the attack.

drugs.name: Mannitol 20%
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 g/kg IV over 30 to 60 minutes (lower end in the elderly and in cardiac or renal disease)
drugs.notes: If inadequate response to acetazolamide; check heart and renal function; do not repeat routinely.

drugs.name: Glycerol (oral)
drugs.notes: Alternative to mannitol if not vomiting; avoid in diabetes.
